fields.name: Crossover Stockton
fields.purpose: Crossover investigates where emerging AI, robotics, and human participation could help meet real-world needs in Stockton.

statements.missionQuestion: How can post-scarcity technology solve real problems?
statements.opportunity: As AI and robotics take on more necessary work, we have an extraordinary opportunity: to spend more of our lives caring for one another, other living beings, and the world around us.
statements.startingApproach: We're starting now, investigating real needs in Stockton, taking action, and using what we learn to discover what technology and human participation can make possible.
statements.animalCareVision: What if people who love animals could spend their days rescuing, fostering, training, and rehabilitating dogs, while technology handled more of the paperwork, logistics, and coordination?
statements.animalCareInvestigation: We're investigating what happens to dogs on Stockton's streets, how they reach care, and what gets in the way. We examine public records, check reported conditions firsthand, talk to people already helping, and test pathways to care.
statements.learningRule: What we discover guides what we do next.
statements.presencePractice: We have to show up. Meet people. Observe conditions. Try to help. Discover what happens.
statements.documentationPractice: Crossover connects those experiences through an investigation app: Actions, Activity, Places, and Findings. We document what we do, examine what we learn, and identify what needs investigating next.
statements.aiPractice: AI helps organize the evidence, connect observations, update our findings, and discover new actions. Our articles become a growing body of knowledge that others can use, question, and build upon.
statements.experienceChangesUs: And sometimes the experience changes our understanding. Sometimes it changes us.
statements.publicCommitment: We're investigating real needs in Stockton. Our actions, observations, and findings are public—including what we haven't figured out yet.

biography: Crossover Stockton began with Jeff Kolyer, a former Silicon Valley technology founder exploring the transition from compulsory work to meaningful vocation.

fields.title: Street dogs and access to care
fields.summary: Animal rescuers estimate that hundreds of dogs may be living on Stockton's streets. The city acknowledges recurring shelter overcrowding, while rescue organizations report increasing abandonment and limited capacity to help. The number of dogs currently on the streets, their conditions, and how many are receiving care remain unverified.
what_we_are_seeing: Stockton Animal Services reports recurring shelter-capacity pressure. It prioritizes sick, injured, aggressive, and confirmed abandonment cases, while healthy stray intake generally requires an appointment. Its guidance cautions that a roaming dog may be lost or owned rather than abandoned.
Stockton Street Dogs reports feeding and outreach on the streets several times a week. Its public materials also describe fostering, adoption, and other rescue pathways.

At an October 19, 2026 committee meeting, city officials discussed shelter limitations and repeated roaming-animal violations. The committee advanced proposed animal-control changes for full City Council consideration; the cited report did not establish a final Council outcome.
On October 20, Crossover requested Animal Services field-call records. They were received by email on November 2; their contents and limitations have not yet been assessed here.

what_we_are_seeing: In August 2026, a donation of roughly three semitruck loads, including two loads of frozen food, exceeded Bread of Life's two existing freezers.
Bread of Life reported relying on local partners for refrigerated transportation and temporary cold storage so the donation could still reach residents.
Bread of Life's public materials report distribution through more than 33 locations and service to about 7,000 people per month; these are the organization's reported figures.
Community Partnership for Families also provides neighborhood food distribution and fresh-food access through its Family Resource Centers.

fields.publicName: Dogs on the street in Stockton
fields.title: What would it take to understand the need?
fields.primary_goal: Establish the extent of unmet care needs among dogs on Stockton's streets, understand how existing response and care systems operate, identify where those systems fail to meet needs, and evaluate improvements—including emerging technology—that could produce measurably better outcomes.
fields.introduction: We're investigating where Stockton's street dogs are, what condition they're in, what care reaches them, and which needs remain unmet. Public reports are starting points; records, firsthand observations, and conversations with responders can help us verify what is happening.
fields.findings_summary: Stockton's municipal shelter handles thousands of stray dog intake events, yet the number of dogs currently on the streets and what happens after a dog is reported remain unclear. Our first attempts to volunteer with two animal-care organizations have not yet led to completed onboarding, raising questions about how easily willing residents can get involved. Meanwhile, shelter expansion is underway and additional facilities are proposed, but their impact on access to care remains to be established.

friction-of-volunteering.title: The friction of volunteering
friction-of-volunteering.description: We applied to volunteer with two animal-care organizations. What happens between offering help and actually providing it?

fields.title: The friction of volunteering
fields.description: Crossover's volunteer applications in Stockton raise a practical question: how could better coordination help willingness to care become action?
fields.summary: We applied to volunteer with two animal-care organizations. What happens between offering help and actually providing it?

content.introduction: Wanting to help a dog is only the beginning. A person has to find an opportunity, connect with an organization, complete its requirements, and reach a task they can safely do. Crossover's attempts to volunteer in Stockton give us a starting point for investigating that path.

sections.heading: Two attempts to take part
paragraphs: Crossover submitted a volunteer application to Stockton Street Dogs on October 7, 2026. We had not documented a response as of October 30. We emailed Stockton Animal Services about its Doggie Day Out program on October 12 and submitted a volunteer application in person on October 14. We had not documented a substantive next step by October 30.

These are our firsthand records of two volunteer pathways, not evidence that either organization routinely fails to respond. We do not know what happened to the applications internally or why participation has not progressed. Stockton Animal Services publicly describes volunteer roles and a Doggie Day Out orientation; Stockton Street Dogs also offers a public volunteer entry point. We want to understand what happens after someone uses those entry points.

links.label: Doggie Day Out inquiry Activity record

sections.heading: Where willingness can meet friction
paragraphs: A prospective volunteer finds an organization, applies, and waits to learn the next step. Orientation, training, screening, scheduling, and approval may follow. Some requirements protect animals, volunteers, and the organization and should remain. The question is which parts require human judgment and which repetitive steps could be made easier to understand and complete.

Shelters and rescues are already caring for animals while managing facilities, emergencies, communication, and existing volunteers. Administrative work can consume the same time that could support a new helper. We have not measured these workloads in Stockton or established where any particular application stalled. That is what we need to investigate.

sections.heading: What business already knows
paragraphs: In business, interest is captured and supported. Here we're asking why that kind of smooth pathway isn't available to people who want to help dogs.

Companies have spent decades building systems that answer inquiries, track interest, follow up, schedule appointments, and help people take the next step. An offer to help an animal may still pass through applications, emails, waiting, and manual coordination. This comparison does not treat care as a sale. It asks whether the tools developed to guide commercial participation could also support people who want to care for living beings.

sections.heading: Infrastructure that helps both sides
paragraphs: Stockton Animal Services and Stockton Street Dogs do essential work. Better volunteer infrastructure could help their staff and existing volunteers as well as applicants. It might show which roles are open, explain requirements, acknowledge applications, provide status updates, and make it easier to schedule an appropriate next step. We do not know whether these organizations already use some of these tools or what changes they would find useful.

An AI-supported system could answer routine questions immediately, guide an applicant through forms, coordinate orientation and training, suggest tasks that fit a person's availability and abilities, and reduce repeated administrative work. These are proposals to test with organizations, not claims of a working Stockton system. Screening, animal-handling safeguards, supervision, and final decisions would stay with qualified people. The purpose is to automate the friction surrounding compassion, not compassion itself.

sections.heading: More room for vocation
paragraphs: Today's systems devote substantial effort to making commercial participation easy. AI and automation may make similar coordination tools more accessible to community organizations without requiring large administrative teams. Whether that promise holds for Stockton's animal-care work remains to be tested.

People would still provide attention, judgment, relationships, and direct care. Technology could make it simpler for them to contribute. This is one practical part of Crossover's broader investigation into using new capabilities to free more human time for meaningful work and care.

sections.heading: Questions for the next step
paragraphs: How do these organizations receive and manage volunteer applications? What determines response time, and where do applicants commonly get stuck? Which administrative tasks consume staff and volunteer time? Which steps need human judgment, and which could be simplified? Could organizations share coordination tools while retaining their independence? We need answers from the people doing this work before proposing a specific system.
We've built extraordinary systems for turning interest into purchases. We should be able to build equally effective systems for turning compassion into care.

content.introduction: We appreciate Stockton Animal Services staff for making field-service records available in response to Crossover's October 20 request. The spreadsheet arrived November 2, 2026, and contains 7,183 case records. We began reviewing it November 4. The records give us a new way to examine how reports are classified and closed, but recorded dispositions alone do not establish what happened to each dog. Our review and follow-up questions are ongoing.

sections.heading: Editor's update — November 4, 2026
paragraphs: Since this article was first published on October 30, Stockton Animal Services provided the field-service records Crossover requested on October 20. We received the spreadsheet on November 2 and began reviewing its 7,183 cases on November 4. This article has been revised to reflect that development; conclusions about case classifications, access, and outcomes remain preliminary. We appreciate the department's cooperation and the work involved in making these records available. ♥

Milestones: October 20 — request submitted; October 30 — original article published; November 2 — records received; November 4 — review began. This is a new development, not a correction to the original reporting.

sections.heading: Our October 20 records request
paragraphs: On October 20, Crossover requested approximately 12 months of Stockton Animal Services field-call records involving roaming, stray, abandoned, aggressive, and distressed dogs. We asked for dates, general areas, complaint categories, response dispositions, and closure statuses where maintained. The department supplied a spreadsheet on November 2 containing 7,183 case records. We began reviewing it November 4.

Our questions are which general areas appear in the data, how cases are classified, what the response and closure fields mean, and what can safely be made public. A recorded disposition does not by itself establish an animal's ultimate outcome. We will report what the data supports as we examine it.

sections.heading: What the public can already see
paragraphs: The City provides an online route for animal-related complaints, a list of pets currently in shelter care, and a lost-and-found pet map. Stockton's open-data portal also publishes an animal-shelter overview of intake and outcomes. These are useful public resources. A shelter intake or outcome total, however, is different from a record of each street report and what happened afterward.

Our question is whether a person can follow the path from a reported dog to an officer response, a located animal, care, reunification, placement, or an unresolved case. We have not established that this information is unavailable elsewhere. We are comparing the newly supplied case records with the public tools and considering what can be shared safely before concluding that a gap exists.

sections.heading: Information across organizations
paragraphs: Animal Services is one part of the response. Stockton Street Dogs, independent rescuers, volunteers, and other groups also encounter dogs and provide care. We do not know how their internal records are kept or how they share information. Public access is a separate question: can a resident identify a current need and a safe way to help without relying on an outdated post or an uncertain contact route?

Crossover applied to volunteer with Stockton Street Dogs on October 7. We had not documented a response by October 30. That experience tells us about our own attempt to connect; it does not establish how the organization handles other applications or communicates internally. We want to learn which public and organizational channels already work, and where information about opportunities or outcomes is hard to find.

sections.heading: What better information could make possible
paragraphs: A public, AI-supported animal-welfare information system is a possibility to test. It could organize public reports and official information, show patterns across general areas, record what happened after reports, identify unresolved needs, and connect people with verified ways to help. It could also make investigation findings easier to inspect. This would require cooperation, reliable source data, and a clear account of what each record does and does not establish.

Sensitive animal locations and personal information should be protected. Reported sightings must remain distinct from verified conditions and confirmed outcomes. AI could help sort and summarize information, but people would need to check its work and make care decisions. We have not built or validated such a system for Stockton.

sections.heading: How Crossover is testing the approach
paragraphs: Crossover's public investigation follows a cycle: planned Actions identify what needs checking; Activity records what happened; Findings explain what the evidence supports; new Actions follow from what we learn. Anyone can inspect those pages without creating an account. The October 20 records request and November 2 receipt are documented Activities. Review of the spreadsheet began November 4.

This is an emerging way to make our own work inspectable, not a claim that we have solved coordination across organizations. We are examining field-call classifications and resolution labels, comparing the records with existing public resources, asking responders what information they can share, and testing whether that information helps people act safely.

sections.heading: What remains to establish
paragraphs: We still need to learn what the supplied field-call data can establish, how a public report moves through response and closure, what useful information is already public, and how Animal Services and independent caregivers coordinate when appropriate. The 7,183 case records require careful review; case labels must not be treated as verified animal outcomes. We also need to ask whether better access would change outcomes for dogs, while respecting privacy and safety.
How could better public information and AI-supported coordination help more dogs reach care?

fields.title: What if caring for Stockton's dogs were as easy as going to the park?
fields.description: An investigation into existing dog-care services, proposed facilities, and how more people might participate in caring for Stockton's dogs.
fields.summary: Stockton's shelter is expanding and Streetdogs has proposed a Canine Campus. What would make everyday participation in dog care easier?

content.introduction: Caring for Stockton's dogs already takes public workers, rescue groups, volunteers, and adopters. We are investigating what more could become possible if a welcoming place made it easier for ordinary people to help. This is a question about adding ways to care, alongside the essential services that already exist.

sections.heading: What exists: Stockton Animal Services
paragraphs: Stockton Animal Services performs essential municipal work: responding to animal-control needs, taking animals into the shelter, caring for them, and helping them reach adoption or other outcomes. Its ongoing expansion is a positive development. City plans include treatment, isolation, rehabilitation, and public adoption space; we do not yet know how much additional usable capacity it will provide or how outcomes will change.

On October 14, Crossover visited the shelter at 1575 S. Lincoln Street, submitted a volunteer application, and spoke briefly with staff. We observed construction beside the entrance and a crowded public lobby during our visit. The entrance was difficult for us to find amid the work. The shelter sits in an industrial area, so we are also checking what transportation and walking options would make volunteer outings practical. These are observations from one visit, not a judgment about the shelter or its location. The expansion may address some of the limitations we saw.

links.label: City of Stockton shelter expansion announcement

sections.heading: What is proposed: the Canine Campus
paragraphs: Stockton Streetdogs proposes a Canine Campus that could shelter hundreds of stray dogs at a time, provide overflow space for Stockton Animal Services, and include recovery space for spay and neuter procedures and for sick dogs. Its published proposal describes 24-hour staffing, coordination with rescues, selected volunteers, and opportunities for the public to visit and help. These are the organization's plans, not services operating today.

Streetdogs opened a construction fundraiser in July 2026. Fundraising is documented, but we have not verified full funding, a secured site, approvals, an opening date, or usable operating capacity. If built and staffed, the campus could complement the municipal shelter with more room for recovery, exercise, and care. We want to learn how its public participation plans would work in practice before assuming they would match the broader idea explored below.

sections.heading: A different model: The Asher House
paragraphs: Lee Asher's animal sanctuary in Oregon offers another model to study. The Asher House says it rescues and rehabilitates animals, places many for adoption, and gives others a lasting home. Animals have room for activity and enrichment; a staff team helps provide care. The nonprofit says donations and merchandise sales support animal care, while Lee purchased the land with personal income.

The Asher House is not currently open for public visits and says it does not yet have a volunteer program. Its animal-centered living environment, rehabilitation work, and adoption network are worth studying for Stockton. A public place where visitors regularly help care for dogs would be an additional local idea, not a description of how The Asher House operates today.

links.label: The Asher House and its operating model

sections.heading: What if helping felt like going to the park?
paragraphs: Here is Crossover's proposal to investigate: a welcoming dog-care place with easy parking, walking trails, open grounds, and comfortable spaces for animals. Someone could arrive, learn which dogs are ready for interaction, and take a suitable dog for a supervised walk. Others could help socialize dogs, assist with rehabilitation under trained guidance, or support daily care.

The goal is to make caring for dogs as accessible as visiting a public park. Access would still need appropriate screening, training, supervision, animal-behavior assessment, and safeguards for dogs and people. We do not yet know what site, staffing, costs, partnerships, and rules would make this workable in Stockton.

sections.heading: More time for care
paragraphs: AI and automation could help with scheduling, matching people to suitable tasks, keeping care records current, and coordinating transport and follow-up. Robotics may eventually help with repetitive physical chores. These are possibilities to test, not tools we have shown to work here. People and animal-care professionals would still make welfare and safety decisions.

If technology reduces the logistical burden, more human time could go toward walking, socializing, rehabilitating, and caring for living beings. That is part of Crossover's broader investigation into a future in which people can spend more of their lives on vocation rather than compulsory work. The immediate test is practical: can more dogs get good care, and can more people take part safely?

sections.heading: The question ahead
paragraphs: We want to learn from Stockton Animal Services, Stockton Streetdogs, other rescuers, and residents: which roles are already open to the public, what barriers keep people from participating, and what extra space or support would genuinely help? The shelter expansion and the Canine Campus proposal are concrete developments to follow. The park-like care setting is a further possibility to examine with the people doing the work.
What would it take to make caring for Stockton's dogs as accessible as visiting a public park?

fields.title: Where are the stray dogs, and how many are there?
fields.description: An ongoing investigation into the number and distribution of dogs on Stockton's streets, starting with published reports and two planned field investigations.
fields.summary: Published estimates suggest hundreds of dogs may be on Stockton's streets. Where are they, and what can firsthand observations establish?

content.introduction: How many dogs are on Stockton's streets, and where are they? Published reports describe abandoned and roaming dogs, but no verified current citywide street-dog count has been established. Crossover is gathering evidence, checking specific areas, and documenting what we actually find. This article starts with what is known and will be updated as our investigation produces firsthand reports.

sections.heading: What the published reports tell us
paragraphs: In an April 6, 2026 CBS Sacramento report, Stockton Street Dogs founder Jesse Mejia estimated that at least 200 to 300 dogs were on Stockton's streets at a given time, potentially rising to 400 during puppy season. Those figures are Mejia's estimates, not an independently verified census. The report and accompanying television coverage are useful leads, but they cannot establish current dog locations or numbers.

Stockton Animal Services recorded 3,106 stray dog intake events in 2024 across its broader multi-jurisdiction service area. Intake events over a year are not a count of dogs currently on Stockton's streets, and cannot be directly compared with the advocate's point-in-time estimate.

links.label: CBS Sacramento: abandoned dogs in Stockton (April 6, 2026)
Investigation question: Where are the stray dogs, and how many are there?

sections.heading: First investigation area: St. Mary's–Church Street corridor
paragraphs: CBS Sacramento reported on June 8, 2026 that Stockton Street Dogs distributed about 200 pounds of food to around 70 dogs during an outreach visit at a Church Street encampment near St. Mary's Community Services. This describes a particular reported event, not the number of dogs currently living in the area. It does not place the dogs at the community-services campus itself.

Crossover plans an initial observation on Monday, November 2, 2026, of a manageable portion of public areas in the St. Mary's–Church Street corridor. We will record the date, general area examined, approximate number of visible dogs (including zero), observed circumstances, and limitations. No Crossover field observation of this corridor is claimed yet. Dogs with unhoused people must not automatically be described as abandoned.

links.label: CBS Sacramento: Church Street outreach report (June 8, 2026)
Planned St. Mary's corridor field action
St. Mary's–Church Street corridor location record

sections.heading: Second investigation area: Carrie Street levee and South Stockton / District 5
paragraphs: The Carrie Street levee near Weston Ranch is a separate location lead, associated with a reported April 2026 roaming-dog incident. September reporting separately described increased stray- and dumped-dog encounters across District 5, but did not identify Carrie Street as the location of those encounters. These reports are not evidence of how many dogs are there now.

Crossover plans to select a safe public observation route, examine conditions firsthand, and document its observations—including zero dogs if none are found. This visit has not yet happened. We will not treat a historical report as a current location or publish precise sensitive animal or resident locations.

links.label: Planned South Stockton / District 5 field action
Carrie Street levee / Weston Ranch location record

sections.heading: What remains unknown
paragraphs: We do not yet have a verified current citywide population estimate or a reliable map of where dogs are present. Reports concern different dates, areas, and kinds of observations, and dogs seen roaming may be owned, lost, abandoned, or living with people. These categories cannot be inferred from appearance or location alone.
Even visits to two areas will not constitute a citywide census. They can establish limited, dated firsthand observations that help us test published leads and plan a better investigation.

sections.heading: Follow the investigation
paragraphs: This is an ongoing article, not a completed conclusion. The St. Mary's corridor and South Stockton / District 5 actions are currently planned; their field observations are not yet available. When firsthand reports are completed, we will add dated results, sources, limitations, and any resulting changes to our findings. New evidence may change our questions and where we investigate next.
The number and location of Stockton's street dogs remain unknown. That's precisely why we're going to look.

active.description: Publication eligibility for the current Need index and related public updates. It does not describe severity, investigation progress, or whether the underlying condition persists or improves.

organization_ids.label: Organizations
organization_ids.description: Organizations related to this record. On outside evidence this is a reference, not evidence of Crossover contact.

map_reference_location_ids.label: Nearby geographic references
map_reference_location_ids.description: Nearby public geographic references for an action. These are not necessarily action sites or observed animal locations.

investigation_status.label: investigation_status
investigation_status.description: Crossover's investigative engagement with this need, not its severity, priority, condition trend, or solution outcome. Identified means the need is recorded; investigating means Crossover is actively examining it.

visualGuidance.preferredAssets: Preferred images and logos express a preference, not layout instructions. A renderer may use an appropriate alternative or no image.
visualGuidance.descriptions: Visual and logo descriptions describe an intended subject or identity; they are not alt text. Alt text must describe the image actually shown.
visualGuidance.evidence: Illustrative or generated imagery is not investigation evidence. Documentary images retain separate source, attribution, and caption information.
visualGuidance.logos: Do not present an invented logo as an organization's official logo.
visualGuidance.needInvestigationStatus: For Needs, Identified may be shown in gray and Investigating in green. These describe Crossover's inquiry, not severity or improvement.

browseGuidance.defaultView: Open browseable records with All types in one flat list, newest first by dateForSort.value. Preserve the mixed types unless the visitor filters or groups them.
browseGuidance.filtering: Search and type filters retain the same newest-first order. Put undated records after dated records; break equal-date ties by stable record ID ascending. Do not invent a date for an undated record.
browseGuidance.dateMeaning: dateForSort.field identifies what the date means. An occurrence, source publication, completion, record update, review, verification, and period date are distinct; label the selected field when displaying the date. dateForSort is a browse key, not a claim that every record was published or changed that day.

locationGuidance.presentation: For a Location with a nonempty map_reference.query, show a prominent Open in Google Maps link alongside its internal Crossover record link. Generate the URL from the query; do not store a duplicate URL on every record.
locationGuidance.precision: map_reference.precision describes the geographic search term, not a verified event, dog, person, or current condition. Corridors and general areas must be presented as broad references. map_reference.verified means the place name or address itself has a documented source; it does not verify associated reports.
locationGuidance.embeddedMaps: map_reference.embed_url is a Google Maps Share > Embed a map URL for a verified street address. Show it with the precision warning and Open in Google Maps link. Keep broad or unverified geographic references as search links rather than pinned embeds.
